query: Consider the following context: Refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) are promising candidates for next-generation nuclear applications, particularly fusion reactors, due to their excellent high-temperature mechanical properties and irradiation resistance. In that context, which material can be used for low-activation structural material for high-temperature plasma-facing components (PFCs) in fusion reactors, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) that incorporates low-activation elements can serve as a structural material for high‐temperature plasma‐facing components in fusion reactors, combining tungsten’s high melting point and low sputter erosion with the enhanced radiation resistance and reduced long-term activation provided by the high-entropy design.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast or additively manufactured tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy with a homogeneous, solid-solution microstructure.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to high-temperature fusion reactor conditions including exposure to deuterium–tritium plasma, high heat flux, and neutron irradiation.
generation.conditions: Operation at elevated temperatures (≥1000 K) under simultaneous plasma exposure and irradiation conditions typical of fusion reactor divertor regions.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of coherent nanoprecipitates and a refined, radiation-tolerant grain structure that result from the high configurational entropy of the alloy.
generation.mechanism: High-entropy mixing reduces the thermodynamic driving force for defect formation and slows atomic diffusion, limiting radiation-induced microstructural degradation. Tungsten’s intrinsic properties provide high-temperature stability and low sputtering, while the alloy’s tailored composition minimizes activation by avoiding elements that produce long-lived radionuclides.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to conventional tungsten, the RHEA will show improved mechanical stability, reduced erosion and tritium retention, and lower radioactive activation after irradiation, thus extending the operational lifetime of plasma-facing components.
generation.baseline: Performance metrics (oxidation resistance, mechanical integrity, tritium retention, and activation levels) of current tungsten-based PFC materials under similar high-temperature and irradiation conditions.
generation.boundary: The benefits are expected to hold under high-temperature (≥1000 K) and high neutron/ion flux regimes typical for divertor environments, but performance may be composition and processing dependent.
generation.uncertainty: The exact alloy composition needed to balance ultra-high strength, ductility, oxidation resistance, and low activation remains to be optimized, and processing effects (e.g., nanoprecipitation control) introduce uncertainties in long-term behavior under fusion conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one of the tungsten-based RHEA and one using state‐of‐the‐art conventional tungsten for plasma-facing components. Expose both sets to simulated fusion reactor conditions (high temperature ≥1000 K, deuterium–tritium plasma, and neutron irradiation) in a controlled irradiation chamber over a relevant timescale. Post-exposure, evaluate microstructural changes (grain size, defect density, nanoprecipitate formation), mechanical properties (strength, ductility), oxidation resistance, and the level of induced radioactivity (activation).
measurements: Mechanical strength and ductility via tensile/compression tests
Oxidation resistance via high-temperature oxidation tests
Radioactivity measurements using gamma spectroscopy or other activation analysis techniques
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tungsten-based RHEA does not exhibit statistically significant improvements in mechanical stability, oxidation resistance, and (importantly) reduced activation compared to the conventional tungsten samples under the test conditions, or if it shows a degradation in any critical performance metric, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) first appeared in public view in 2010 [ [1] ]. Thereafter, they aroused great concern from researchers at home and abroad. Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [7] , [8] , [9] ]. Clean energy production is the cornerstone of our time. Options for sustainable clean energy include advanced power generation systems that have the potential to drastically reduce the emission of greenhouse gases. These advanced systems are often required to operate under harsh conditions to optimize efficiency, which poses several challenges for the available materials. An example of advanced power system is one that is associated with fusion energy [1] . Beyond traditional fission-based systems, fusion reactors not only promise nearly unlimited clean energy, but also avoid the generation of long-life radioactive waste produced in fission devices. One remaining challenge is that of materials, which can withstand extreme conditions of radiation, temperature, and stress, with long-term steady properties for the power plant to be economically viable [2] – [4] . A key component in current tokamak designs is the divertor, which will be in contact with the deuterium-tritium (D-T) plasma and sustain severe fluxes of particles (helium (He) ash, D and T) and heat, along with radiation damage induced by high-energy neutrons [2] , [3] . Key components in magnetic fusion reactors, such as the divertor or the plasma-facing materials (PFMs), are required to have stringent properties including low activation, high melting point, good thermomechanical properties, low sputter erosion, and low tritium retention/codeposition. They must operate at high temperature (≥1000 K) for long durations (>10 7 s), without failure or extensive erosion while exposed to large plasma heat and an intense mixture of ionized and energetic neutral species of hydrogen isotopes (D and T), He ash (fluxes, >10 24 m −2 s −1 ), and neutrons ( [1] ). Tungsten (W) is the leading PFM candidate because of its high melting temperature, low erosion rates, and small tritium retention. These advantages are unfortunately coupled with very low fracture toughness characterized by brittle transgranular and intergranular failure regimes, which severely restrict the useful operating temperature window and also create a range of fabrication difficulties. Furthermore, blistering at moderate temperature (<800 K) by D and He ( [2] , [3] ) and the formation of pits, holes, and bubbles by He at higher temperature (>1600 K) ( [4] ) have all been observed.
